title: Bank of America warns of 2027 stock market risk few expect
detail:
Bank of America warns of 2027 stock market risk few expect
Moz Farooque, Aparajita Chatterjee
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 9:47 AM PDT 5 min read
^GSPC
BAC
Trade BAC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Anyone checking their 401(k) this fall could be forgiven for thinking Wall Street has shaken off its worries.

The S&P 500 ended October 22 at 7,623.68, up 11.4% for the year and just 2.5% below its October 6 record. More recently, however, the rally has lost some steam. After three years of AI-fueled gains, the S&P 500 has managed a more modest 3% advance over the past three months.

For investors who stayed in the market through its twists and turns, those are comforting numbers as they look toward 2027.

But in a note shared with me, Bank of America's Michael Hartnett sees a major problem hiding behind the gains.

As we all know, the AI boom that has helped power stocks depends on extraordinary spending on chips, data centers, and electricity. Much of that expansion touches the bond market, where borrowing costs are rising and lenders are getting choosier.

Hartnett worries investors are overlooking what happens if that money becomes harder to raise. In Bank of America's October survey, which was shared with me, just 6% of fund managers expected a hard economic landing.

He sees three possible paths for 2027, including one that could leave stock market investors painfully exposed.

Bank of America says AI financing pressures could threaten stocks during 2027.
Michael M. Santiago / Getty Images
Bank of America warns AI financing could threaten stocks in 2027

Wall Street's still betting the house on AI heading into 2027, but Michael Hartnett feels it's overlooking the enormous cost of keeping the boom alive.

More Bank of America:

BofA splits software into winners and losers as AI agents arrive

Bank of America reveals hidden moat that makes Morgan Stanley a buy

Bank of America resets Amazon stock forecast on delivery plan

For perspective, BofA semiconductor analyst Vivek Arya estimates spending by major cloud companies could climb from a whopping $860 billion in 2026 to $1.2 trillion in 2027, nearly 40% growth as reported by Biggo. Moreover, to finance that tremendous investment in chips and energy infrastructure, businesses are turning to debt markets.

Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL), Meta Platforms (META), and Oracle (ORCL) issued $194 billion in bonds through July 7, Reuters reported, compared with $108 billion throughout 2025, and that dependence on borrowing is precisely what worries Hartnett.

He warns that hyperscaler bond spreads widening beyond 200 basis points, or two percentage points above comparable benchmark yields, could trigger forced selling and broader financial stress.

Lenders are already distinguishing between borrowers.

JPMorgan's October analysis identified credit-default swap spreads of 50 to 120 basis points for financially stronger AI companies, versus roughly 300 basis points for some infrastructure borrowers and 1,100 basis points for a heavily leveraged borrower.

Building wealth over a decade often comes down to owning companies that ride a long-lasting trend, and artificial intelligence (AI) spending is one of the biggest. Research firm Gartner expects worldwide AI spending to reach about $2.7 trillion in 2026 and climb to roughly $3.6 trillion in 2027.

CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD), Snowflake (NYSE: SNOW), and Dell Technologies (NYSE: DELL) are competitively positioned to capitalize on that opportunity. While the S&P 500 has returned 13% year to date, these stocks have delivered far superior returns. Here's why they are still worth buying and holding for 10 years.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

CrowdStrike

CrowdStrike's Falcon platform protects businesses from cyberattacks across their cloud systems and user accounts, and growing demand for AI-powered security solutions is fueling its momentum. The stock has doubled this year as management called the second quarter its "best quarter" in history, with net new annual recurring revenue accelerating to 51% year-over-year growth in the fiscal second quarter of 2027.

CrowdStrike's edge is its data. Its platform analyzes about 7 trillion events a day. Management says the company has been labeling this data for a decade, providing it with information that competitors don't have. That advantage shows up in a high subscription-adjusted gross profit margin of 81%.

Management sees a lot more growth ahead. CrowdStrike hit $5.2 billion in ARR in fiscal 2026, and expects full-year fiscal 2027 ARR to reach between $6.3 billion and $6.6 billion. Management now expects to hit its long-term targets one year ahead of schedule, reaching $10 billion in ARR by fiscal 2030 and $20 billion by fiscal 2035.

The stock trades at about 40 times this fiscal year's expected revenue. That's a steep premium, but it reflects a highly profitable business that saw accelerating net new ARR last quarter and a path to more than tripling its ARR over the next decade.

Image source: Getty Images.
Snowflake

Snowflake runs a cloud platform where companies store and analyze their data and build AI applications on top of it. The stock is up about 46% this year as product revenue growth accelerated for the third straight quarter, reaching 37% year over year in the latest quarter (ended July 31).

Companies using Snowflake can pull all their data into one place and control who can access it. This makes it easier for companies to build and run AI agents. The platform is not easy to build, and that edge supports strong profitability, with Snowflake earning a high adjusted gross profit margin of 75%.

title: Cathie Wood buys $24.5 million of tumbling megacap stock
detail:
Cathie Wood buys $24.5 million of tumbling megacap stock
Silin Chen, Celine Provini
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 10:07 AM PDT 7 min read

^GSPC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Cathie Wood, chief of Ark Investment Management, often buys her favorite tech stocks when their prices fall.

That's what she's doing with Meta Platforms (META), adding shares after the Facebook parent's stock tumbled following its earnings report.

Last year, the flagship Ark Innovation ETF gained 35.49%, far outpacing the S&P 500's return of 17.88% in the same period. So far this year, Wood's flagship Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK) is up 6.59% as of Oct. 23, while the S&P 500 surged 11.37%.

Wood gained a reputation after the Ark Innovation ETF delivered a rosy 153% return in 2020. But her style also brings painful losses in bearish markets, as seen in 2022, when the ETF tumbled more than 60%.

Those swings have weighed on Wood's long-term gains. As of Oct. 23, her Ark Innovation ETF has delivered a five-year annualized return of -6.83%, while the S&P 500 has an annualized return of 10.9% over the same period, according to data from Morningstar.

Cathie Wood remains optimistic about AI and tech revolution

Wood focuses on high-tech companies across artificial intelligence, blockchain, biomedical technology, and robotics. She believes these businesses have strong growth potential, but their volatility often causes fluctuations in the Ark's funds.

Over the decade ended 2025, the Ark Innovation ETF wiped out nearly $5 billion in investor wealth, according to a report by Morningstar's analyst Amy Arnott. That made it the fourth-biggest wealth destroyer among mutual funds and ETFs in the ranking. 

Wood defended her investment strategy after an audience member at a recent summit questioned ARK's performance compared with the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ).

Related: Cathie Wood sells $16 million of surging tech stock

"Investors deserve to understand both their returns and the decisions behind them," Wood said in an Oct. 5 post on X.

She argued that the ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) and QQQ are built differently. QQQ tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, while ARK actively invests in companies it believes are driving disruptive innovation across industries, including healthcare, financial services, and transportation.

Wood has long been optimistic about AI, which she sees as a major driver of productivity, economic growth, and corporate profits in the years ahead. She has also pushed back against recent fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

In September, Wood reposted a post by David Sacks on X, saying he makes a good case that the "AI will kill humanity" headlines were orchestrated.

Coca-Cola (NYSE: KO) has delivered for investors this year. The stock has scored total returns of 35% since the beginning of the year. That is well above the 14% total return of the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC), an unusual performance for a mature company accustomed to single-digit revenue growth.

As a result, Coca-Cola stock is having its best year since 1996. Still, even though its performance could continue, the stock's growth could face a roadblock in its archrival, PepsiCo. Here's how.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

PepsiCo's total return for 2026 is around -3%, far below Coca-Cola's. Still, despite that performance, PepsiCo's stock is becoming the better buy on just about every level.

KO Total Return Level data by YCharts

Admittedly, PepsiCo reported negligible revenue growth for years as consumer tastes shifted away from its products. However, improvements began in fiscal 2025 as it cut prices on some items and added healthier ingredients to its products.

That shift should highlight PepsiCo's increasingly attractive financials, and its revenue growth was 6% in its latest quarter, close to Coca-Cola's 7%.

That is likely not enough of a difference to justify Coca-Cola's considerable valuation premium. Currently, it trades at 29 times earnings, far above PepsiCo's P/E ratio of 17. Moreover, PepsiCo's dividend yield of 4.2% is meaningfully higher than Coca-Cola's 2.2%. Even though Coca-Cola's 64-year dividend increase streak is longer than PepsiCo's at 54 years, both hold Dividend King status, meaning companies that have increased their payouts for 50 years or more.

This is not to say that Coca-Cola is a sell. Coca-Cola owns over 200 beverage brands that remain popular globally, and analysts forecast 4% revenue growth during 2026. That is likely enough to keep the more conservative, income-oriented shareholders in Coca-Cola stock.

Nonetheless, PepsiCo's improvements make its lower P/E ratio and higher dividend yield more attractive. That factor alone suggests that Coca-Cola could struggle to attract additional buyer interest.

title: Zero-Day Option Traders Are Betting Against Big S&P 500 Swings
detail:
Zero-Day Option Traders Are Betting Against Big S&P 500 Swings
Bloomberg · Source: UBS Derivatives Strategy
Christian Dass
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 7:00 AM PDT 5 min read
^GSPC

(Bloomberg) -- While some investors position for AI earnings, geopolitics and interest rates to send stocks either to new highs or into a tailspin, zero-day option traders have increasingly bet that the S&P 500 Index will remain calm.

Most Read from Bloomberg

Trump Prepares for Iran Escalation After US, Israeli Polls

Bitcoin Billionaires Are Racing to Ride a 3,000% Crypto Boom

Amazon's New Tablet Is a Credible iPad Rival for Much Less Money

Secretive Ukrainian Deep-Strike Unit Behind Rapid Expansion of Deep-Strike Campaign

Indonesia Begins Trimming Pipeline Gas Exports to Singapore

An analysis of 0DTE options flow from UBS Group AG derivatives strategist Kieran Diamond shows a marked shift toward tactical traders buying calls and selling puts when the market declines, and doing the opposite during rallies. The net effect of what they term a "counter-trend delta bias" is the equivalent of buying low and selling high, which further suppresses swings on the S&P 500.

Zero-day to expiry options have taken on an outsized importance in the daily moves of the equities gauge, with around 66% of the overall volume expiring within a day, according to Garrett DeSimone at OptionMetrics. That's increased the focus on short-term positioning as both retail and institutional traders seek insight on how options flows are influencing the $66 trillion US benchmark index.

"This counter-trend trading pattern seems to be a response to very rangebound markets," said Diamond. "The magnitude of these options flows means that this can start to look self-fulfilling, with options investors helping to limit price moves in either direction."

This intraday tactical shift since 2024 is notable, with larger volumes trading on smaller moves, helping limit S&P 500 realized volatility. The pattern resembles the stabilizing effect of positive gamma, with traders buying into dips and selling into rallies, much like option dealers who are long gamma and similarly buy declines and sell rallies to stay delta-neutral.

The counter-trend trading bias is one factor that has helped contain moves. Another is the long option-dealer gamma regime often seen in the S&P 500, much of which is driven by the prevalence of a big institutional trader selling one-day iron condors — a put spread and a call spread.

RELATED: Popular Zero-Day Trades Curb Stock Rallies: Options Watch

The growth of the 0DTE counter-trend trading flow is now so great that the net effect outweighs the impact from the option dealer re-hedging, according to UBS.

History Says This ETF Could Be the Biggest Winner of the Stock Market Sell-Off

With nearly 10 months of 2026 in the books, it's fair to say that this year hasn't been easy for equity investors, but they've been rewarded for taking risks. The Nasdaq-100 and S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) are up 14.6% and 11.7%, respectively, year to date, confirming market participants are being compensated for enduring equity market turbulence.

Those data points also confirm that broader indexes aren't in corrections, let alone bear markets. Still, bear markets and deep pullbacks are facts of investing life. Rather than timing the market, which is a tall, often fruitless order, smart investors use sell-offs as opportunities to build shopping lists or add to existing positions that may have been overly punished.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

This Vanguard sector has a history of bouncing back following sell-offs. Image source: Getty Images.

Investors who want a potential rebound candidate following a still-theoretical market sell-off may want to keep a close eye on the Vanguard Information Technology ETF (NYSEMKT: VGT).

Recent history vindicates VGT

This $149 billion Vanguard fund, the largest dedicated technology exchange-traded fund (ETF), offers investors recent post-sell-off behavior. Like other sectors, tech tumbled immediately after the onset of the war in Iran, but the pullback was short-lived, and this tech ETF rebounded sharply.

Then in July, the bears again came calling for tech, sending the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index into a bear market in less than a month and to its swiftest correction since the tech bubble popped in 2026. The effects of semiconductor stocks on this Vanguard ETF can't be understated because the fund devotes 43.6% of its weight to chipmakers and equipment names. The point is, even with some unnerving dips this year, this tech ETF is still up 28%.

Of course, predicting the cause of the next correction or bear market isn't easy, but some hints may be emerging today. Those include the Federal Reserve's battle with inflation, waged through higher interest rates. The Fed needs to strike a delicate balance between cooling consumer costs while not threatening economic growth.

It's admittedly speculative for now, but let's assume that higher interest rates blunt economic activity, forcing broader equity indexes to decline materially. This Vanguard tech ETF would likely suffer in the immediate aftermath of that scenario, but as market participants reconcile that economic growth could be sluggish for an extended period, growth stocks, including many of this ETF's components, are likely to become more appealing.

title: Apollo’s Torsten Slok Warns AI Has Delivered ‘Zero Financial Payoff’ Outside Tech — 'AI Story Will Be Decided In The S&P 493, Not The Mag 7'
detail:
Apollo’s Torsten Slok Warns AI Has Delivered ‘Zero Financial Payoff’ Outside Tech — 'AI Story Will Be Decided In The S&P 493, Not The Mag 7'

Slok's data painted a sharp divide between the Magnificent 7 and the other 493 companies in the S&P 500.

Revenue per employee has climbed significantly for the Magnificent 7, reaching roughly $780,000 on an inflation-adjusted basis, while revenue per employee for the S&P 493 remains around $525,000.

Slok noted that the same pattern appears in profit margins. Margins for the Magnificent 7 have climbed to nearly 30%, while margins for the S&P 493 remain around 10%.

Artificial intelligence has become one of the biggest investment themes in markets, with companies pouring billions of dollars into chips, data centers, software and AI models. But according to Apollo Global Management Chief Economist Torsten Slok, the much-discussed AI payoff has yet to show up across most of corporate America.

Slok argued in a note on Saturday that the gap between technology companies and the broader S&P 500 is becoming increasingly important for investors. While the Magnificent 7 are seeing stronger revenue per worker and expanding profit margins, the rest of the index has yet to show a comparable improvement.

Slok Warns AI Has Yet To Boost Revenue, Margins Or Productivity

Slok's data painted a sharp divide between the Magnificent 7 and the other 493 companies in the S&P 500.

Revenue per employee has climbed significantly for the Magnificent 7, reaching roughly $780,000 on an inflation-adjusted basis, while revenue per employee for the S&P 493 remains around $525,000.

Slok noted that the same pattern appears in profit margins. Margins for the Magnificent 7 have climbed to nearly 30%, while margins for the S&P 493 remain around 10%.

The economist highlighted that the bigger question is whether AI is translating into broader productivity gains. Slok's productivity data shows no clear acceleration in total factor productivity growth despite the rapid adoption and investment in AI.

"Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech," he said.

Slok added that this leaves the broader corporate sector facing a difficult question: if AI is supposed to transform business, when will that transformation show up in revenue, margins and productivity?

AI Spending Is Concentrated And So Is The Payoff, Says Slok

Slok added that one reason the macroeconomic impact may remain limited is that AI spending itself is highly concentrated.

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) has been one of the most successful artificial intelligence (AI) stocks on the market. It's up more than 1,000% over the past three years, although it's up only a modest 10% year-to-date, roughly in line with the S&P 500.

If you were lucky enough to invest $10,000 in Palantir stock on its first day of trading in 2020, you'd have around $212,000 today. But where could a $10,000 investment today possibly take you?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Why Palantir is one of the hottest AI stocks

Palantir is different from most other hot AI stocks because it doesn't make any of the parts, like Nvidia or Micron, and it doesn't support the build-out, like CoreWeave or Bloom Energy. Instead, it uses AI to help organizations and businesses unify different databases to detect patterns and make informed decisions.

Palantir's platform gives users an edge over the competition, and it's attracting more and more business as clients see real value. At some point, it's going to become the baseline for working, because it will be hard to compete without it.

It also has a unique working model. It customizes each client's interface based on its unique needs, and either brings in the company's team for a "bootcamp" or, in certain cases, sends its own engineers into a client's business.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Palantir has several products. Its original platform, Gotham, was created to help defense and law enforcement analyze data, while Foundry does similar things for commercial enterprises. Its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) brings AI models and agents into the operations to pull it all together.

Growth has been spectacular as organizations realize what these kinds of features can do for them. Total revenue increased 93% year over year in the second quarter, driven by a 149% increase in the U.S. commercial business, which now accounts for 81% of the business. It closed 220 deals worth at least $1 million and 73 deals worth at least $10 million, all of which are multiyear contracts that generate annual revenue.

It's also highly profitable. The adjusted operating margin was 62% in the quarter, and earnings per share (EPS) increased from $0.13 to $0.41.

Risks and opportunities

How much higher can it go? The market obviously thinks a lot more, considering how expensive the stock is. It trades at a trailing P/E ratio of 167 and a price-to-sales ratio of 81, making it the most expensive stock in the S&P 500 by that metric.
